## Active

### D-020 — Login returns a best-effort profile so the UI can set the language

> _2026-08-21 · realm/blong-login · active_

`login.token.create/restore/refresh` resolve the user profile through a new configurable
`profileGet` login method (default `access.profile.get`) and return `profile: {actorId, language}`.
A missing or disabled `profileGet` NEVER fails login: it silently yields `language: 'en'` and no
profile, so lightweight suites without an access realm are unaffected. `client_credentials` keeps
the hardcoded `'en'` and no profile, because it is a machine credential with no interactive user.

### D-021 — The login profile is response-only, never a token claim

> _2026-08-21 · realm/blong-login · active_

`profile` is deliberately not part of the JWT or the refresh token: `token.ts` destructures it out
of the `...rest` claims spread, so it cannot be smuggled into a token or grow the token payload.
`language` remains a JWT claim — now the resolved preferred language instead of a hardcoded `'en'` —
because the server needs it before the client has any profile.

### D-058 — client_credentials mints no DB session

> _2026-08-20 · realm/blong-login · active_

The question was whether the `client_credentials` grant in `login.token.create` should create a
DB-backed session through `access.session.create`; the answer is no. App tokens are long-lived
machine credentials — no refresh rotation, inactivity tracking or restore cookie applies. The first
attempt did create a session with the application's key as `userId`, which FK-failed
(`access_session.userId` to `access_user.userId`, and apps have no `access_user` row) and broke the
blong-gateway `appToken`/meter flow. `client_credentials` now mints the token and writes the audit
only; sessions are exclusive to interactive password logins. Verified: blong-gateway tap 20/20,
which had been failing on the FK constraint.

### D-065 — blong-login's server config uses blong.type, not typebox

> _2026-08-20 · realm/blong-login · active_

`core/blong-login/server.ts` no longer imports `Type` from typebox; its config-optional helper uses
`blong.type.*` exclusively. Typebox stays the dependency, but the framework-provided `blong.type` is
the access path. Verified: lint green (core/blong, blong-login, blong-access) and tap access 37/37,
gateway 20/20, party 15/15, kopi 6/6.

### D-439 — blong-login names no children, and no layers: the table does it

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-login · active_

This realm predates the well-known layer table and named orchestrator and gateway as explicit
children, then listed them again under every intent that needed them. A folder a realm names as a
child is skipped by layer discovery, so the table could never supply what the realm had claimed, and
removing the per-intent lists alone took login out of the generated tree. Removing the children as
well fixes the cause: discovery finds both folders, the table activates them under microservice, k8s
and upgrade, and the generated suite tree is byte-identical to the one that has always been
deployed. Verified by diffing a fresh generation against the deployed tree, and by the full k3d
cycle afterwards.

## Superseded

### D-438 — The login realm keeps an explicit k8s block, and the tree is the evidence

> _2026-10-07 · realm/blong-login · superseded_

The plan todo called the k8s orchestrator and gateway entries in this realm's server.ts redundant,
since the layer table lists both under k8s. They are not: the realm names those two folders as
explicit children, and layer discovery skips a folder a realm names, so the table never supplies
them and the realm's own config is the only place that can. Removing the block while checking took
login out of the generated suite tree — three deployments instead of four, because the plan
attributes a namespace to a realm through the ports it contributes — and restoring it produced the
tree that has always been deployed. The comment in the file now says this, so the next reader does
not repeat the experiment.

Superseded by the simpler fix the user proposed: the block is gone, and so are the explicit children
that made it necessary. Removing children: `['./orchestrator', './gateway']` lets layer discovery
see the folders, so the table's k8s column activates them and the realm's own microservice and k8s
blocks are redundant. The generated suite tree is byte-identical, which is the check that the
earlier experiment lacked.
